content: Specialist physicians working in hospital settings, such as oncologists or critical care specialists, often manage patients with severe or life-threatening illnesses. According to WHO recommendations, these specialists should have intermediate-level training in palliative care to provide comprehensive care. In high-income countries (HICs), most palliative care is not delivered by palliative care specialists. Instead, general practitioners and family physicians within primary health care (PHC) systems often lead, teach, and practice palliative care. However, the professional designation of the provider is less important than their competencies. Task sharing and task shifting have been shown to be safe and effective strategies to improve access to PHC services, including the management of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, asthma, epilepsy, anxiety, depression, and cancer screening. Additionally, specially trained nurses can administer opioid therapy for moderate to severe pain caused by advanced cancer or AIDS. Non-physician health workers, including community health workers (CHWs), can play significant roles in PHC when appropriately trained and supervised. Universal health coverage (UHC) aims to ensure financial risk protection, access to quality essential health care services, and access to safe, effective, and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all. Achieving UHC is not possible without universal access to PHC, which includes community-based palliative care for pain and symptom management, psychosocial support, and home care for patients with serious illnesses, as well as financial risk protection for their families. In most settings, integrating community-based palliative care into PHC is essential to achieve universal access. The WHO has developed a guide for planners, implementers, and managers to integrate palliative care into community-based PHC. This integration aims to improve patient outcomes by preventing and relieving suffering associated with serious or complex health problems, reducing healthcare system costs by minimizing hospital admissions near the end of life, providing financial risk protection for patients and families, and promoting UHC. The essential package of palliative care for PHC includes a set of safe, effective, inexpensive, off-patent, and widely available medicines; simple and affordable equipment; basic social supports; and the human resources needed to deliver these services effectively and safely. These elements collectively address physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering. Morphine, in oral fast-acting and injectable forms, is the most clinically important medicine in palliative care. It must be accessible to patients with terminal dyspnea or moderate to severe pain, whether acute, chronic, or associated with malignancy. However, opioids should not be the first-line treatment for chronic non-malignant pain outside of palliative or end-of-life care, except under special circumstances with strict monitoring. Physicians providing primary care should be adequately trained and legally empowered to prescribe morphine in any necessary dose to relieve patient suffering. Training in basic palliative care can prepare physicians to prescribe and manage morphine safely and effectively. In some settings, such as Uganda, specially trained and supervised nurses are authorized to prescribe and manage morphine analgesia. Balancing the accessibility of opioids for medical use with minimizing the risk of diversion and illicit use is critical. Hospitals, community health centers (CHCs), and pharmacies should store morphine securely, maintain accurate records, and train personnel in safe storage and recordkeeping. Physicians should also be trained to assess and minimize the risk of opioid dependence and diversion. Other essential palliative care medicines include oral and injectable haloperidol and oral selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like fluoxetine. These medicines, while often considered psychiatric or psychotropic, have multiple essential uses in palliative care. For example, haloperidol is a first-line treatment for nausea, vomiting, agitation, delirium, and anxiety, while SSRIs are used for depression and persistent anxiety. Any primary care physician should be prepared and permitted to prescribe these medicines, not just psychiatrists or neurologists. Patients with severe psychiatric illnesses, such as psychotic or bipolar disorders, should be referred to specialist care whenever possible. Petroleum jelly is essential for dressing non-healable wounds, as it prevents pain and bleeding associated with wet-to-dry dressings. Metronidazole powder, made by crushing metronidazole pills, is crucial for reducing or eliminating the odor of wounds infected with anaerobic bacteria. Equipment such as nasogastric tubes, urinary catheters, pressure-reducing mattresses, locked safeboxes for opioids, flashlights with rechargeable batteries, and adult diapers are necessary for palliative care. These items are inexpensive, simple to use, and essential for relieving physical or psychological suffering. Human resources for palliative care depend on the level and type of healthcare delivery site and the competency of staff in palliative care rather than their professional designations. Medical doctors, clinical officers, or assistant doctors trained in basic palliative care should be capable of preventing or relieving most pain and other physical suffering. They should also be able to diagnose and provide pharmacotherapy for uncomplicated anxiety disorders, depression, or delirium. Nurses, psychologists, social workers, and CHWs can also be trained to provide culturally appropriate psychotherapy for depression. In cases where clinicians encounter suffering they cannot adequately treat, such as pain refractory to escalating morphine doses or depression unresponsive to maximum-dose SSRIs, patients should be referred to higher levels of specialist care. If referral is not possible, clinicians with palliative care training should use available resources, including telemedicine, to provide the best possible care.
